target_only_tests.note: Target-only. lease.ts routes its one nondeterministic call -- the generated fallback action_id in recordRefusal -- through leaseSeams.uuid4Hex (D-0014), so a case needing a pinned id has a way to get one. interlock's own suite never needs it (every case that reaches the refusal path passes its own attempt_id), so this liveness test has no source counterpart and is not counted as ported coverage. It exists because a seam nothing routes through is worse than no seam: it would look like a control point while production went around it.

entries.reason: Three sub-assertions have no literal JS form and are replaced by the strongest faithful version, none weaker. (1) `Sneaky('run')` as the table name: Python's `PROTECTED_TABLES.index(table)` accepts a str subclass by `==` and canonicalises it, so the source asserts the built statement equals the plain-string one; JS `indexOf` is strict so the port REFUSES it (UnfencedStatement) -- asserted as the refusal. The source's property (the caller's object never reaches the template) is still pinned by the plain-string half `statement.startsWith('UPDATE run\n')`. (2) `Sneaky('status')` as a mapping KEY cannot exist: a JS property key is coerced to a primitive string before the object does, so the case asserts that coercion (`Object.keys(...) === ['status']`, typeof 'string') and that the built statement carries `SET status = 'done'`. (3) `type(fence_epoch)()` becomes `new (fenceEpoch.constructor)()`. All other sub-assertions are verbatim.

entries.reason: Deferred one belt while outbox.ts did not exist, and translated in full here. One half is adapted: Python's `Destination` is a runtime_checkable Protocol and therefore a real object in __all__, so the source asserts the package's Destination is not lease's DestinationFencing. The port's Destination is a TypeScript interface -- a compile-time type with no runtime existence -- so that identity comparison has nothing to compare. The runtime stand-in is isDestination, the structural predicate replacing isinstance(x, Destination); asserting on it preserves the property (the destination contract and the lease-side fencing type are separate exported things) against the port's actual runtime surface, and an added assertion pins DestinationFencing's own identity. That the TYPE is exported is proved at compile time by the test file importing it. Every other assertion, including all four about outbox, is translated straight. The entry point is imported BEFORE the outbox module, per the note this ledger carried while the case was deferred: importing outbox first threw, and the assertions below it never ran.

The RUNTIME half is kept and pointed at where a shared mutable default CAN live here: every exported array / plain-object constant of the module must be frozen (so a mutation through one holder throws rather than reaching every other), plus the one field whose source counterpart is the `MappingProxyType({})` default the source docstring names -- `ProtectedWrite.params` -- asserted not shared between two default-built instances and frozen. `leaseSeams` is excluded by name (a seam that could not be replaced would not be a seam). Anti-vacuity: the scanned set must be non-empty.

inherited_limitations.topic: A str-subclass MAPPING KEY cannot reach the builder, so the source's refusal for one has no reachable trigger.
inherited_limitations.status: unconstructible in the target runtime, disclosed
inherited_limitations.detail: The source refuses a str-subclass key in the `set=` mapping with an exact-type gate. JavaScript coerces a property key to a primitive string before the object exists, so the caller's object never reaches the builder at all -- the hole is closed one step earlier than the source closes it. The ported case asserts the coercion rather than assuming it, so the claim is checked rather than argued.

inherited_limitations.topic: requireTable takes the primitive with the built-in valueOf, not with String().
inherited_limitations.status: adapted, and the adaptation is load-bearing
inherited_limitations.detail: Python's `table not in PROTECTED_TABLES` compares by `==`, so a str subclass is accepted and then canonicalised by `.index()` to the closed set's own string. A strict `indexOf` would refuse instead -- the opposite answer, and it would leave that canonicalisation as dead code. The primitive is therefore extracted, but with `String.prototype.valueOf.call`, NOT `String()`: `String()` dispatches through the object's own `toString`, and a hostile subclass overriding `toString` is exactly what this function exists to stop -- the source's own test subclass does that. Python's `str.__eq__` compares the underlying buffer and cannot be reached through `__str__` either, so the built-in call is the faithful analogue as well as the safe one.

inherited_limitations.topic: FencedStatement is a String subclass without the source's __slots__ immutability.
inherited_limitations.detail: interlock's `class FencedStatement(str)` with `__slots__ = ()` cannot be mutated and cannot gain attributes. A JavaScript String subclass can gain properties. Nothing in either suite depends on it.

inherited_limitations.topic: The import-graph scan is weaker than the source's ast walk.
inherited_limitations.detail: `test_no_dependency_edge_on_the_session_provider` uses `ast.parse`, which sees every static import including function-level ones. TypeScript's parse tree is not available at runtime, so the port scans the module source text for ESM specifiers and is blind to a dynamic `import()`. Translated the way migrator.test.ts translates `dir(m)`, with an anti-vacuity assertion so a scan that matched nothing fails rather than passes.

inherited_limitations.topic: resource_of_kind / effect_kind recover a lease's epoch history by decoding a composed kind string.
inherited_limitations.detail: The spike `action` table has no resource column (Q-0001, only partly answered by interlock D-0029), so the composition is the only route. Reproduced verbatim.

inherited_limitations.topic: EpochGuardedDestination is an in-process reference destination, not a durable one.
inherited_limitations.detail: The source documents it as a reference/demo destination; its state is in memory and this module claims nothing else for it.

inherited_limitations.topic: WRITE_HISTORY_QUERY's resource filter is a suffix match, so an '@' inside a resource name makes it ambiguous.
inherited_limitations.detail: The filter is `substr(kind, -(length(:resource) + 1)) = '@' || :resource`, so asking for resource 'r' also returns rows whose kind is 'effect@x@r' -- which belong to resource 'x@r'. Two independently allocated epoch sequences can therefore be mixed in one history read. The SQL is carried byte-identically from interlock, where the query has exactly the same shape, so the port is at parity; the ambiguity is the design's, arising from encoding the resource into the composed `kind` string because the spike `action` table has no resource column (Q-0001). Reproduced rather than repaired, per D-0022. Raised by the Codex review gate (2026-08-22, P2).
